title: The machine room
tagline: How the computer went from a room you walked into, to a rack you owned, to an API you called — each step making the previous one's skills obsolete and its problems permanent.

events.title: IBM System/360
events.byline: Gene Amdahl, Fred Brooks & team, IBM
events.summary: One instruction set across a whole family of machines, so a customer could buy a bigger computer without rewriting their software.
keyPoints: Architecture is separated from implementation — the first time that split is made a product.
Backward compatibility becomes a commercial promise rather than an accident.
The 8-bit byte and general-purpose registers are standardised here.
The software effort produced The Mythical Man-Month, which is its own legacy.
events.impact: Established the stable instruction set as the platform, and made compatibility something vendors compete on. x86 and ARM are still selling the same promise.

events.title: CP-67 and the virtual machine
events.summary: Gives every user their own complete illusory computer, forty years before anyone calls it a cloud.
keyPoints: The hypervisor multiplexes one physical machine into many virtual ones.
Each guest believes it has the hardware to itself, including its own operating system.
Time-sharing turns an expensive machine into a shared utility.
Its descendant, VM/370, is still running today as z/VM.
events.impact: Every idea the cloud is sold on — isolation, multi-tenancy, paying for a slice — was working here first. What changed later was the price and the API, not the concept.

resources.label: Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures

events.title: UNIX
events.byline: Ken Thompson & Dennis Ritchie, Bell Labs
events.summary: Built on a spare machine after a big project was cancelled, and organised around one idea: nearly everything can be a file.
keyPoints: Small programs that do one thing, composed with pipes.
A hierarchical filesystem, with devices and later processes exposed through it.
Rewritten in C in 1973, which made it portable across machines.
Its interfaces outlived its code: POSIX, Linux, and macOS are all downstream.
events.impact: Set the shape of the server. The shell, the process model, the file abstraction, and the composition philosophy are the working environment most infrastructure engineers still live in.

events.title: Ethernet
events.byline: Robert Metcalfe & David Boggs, Xerox PARC
events.summary: Lets machines share one wire by talking whenever they like and coping sensibly when two of them talk at once.
keyPoints: Carrier sense with collision detection: notice the clash, back off randomly, retry.
Randomised exponential backoff — the same pattern every retry policy uses today.
Designed for a shared medium; switching later removed the collisions but kept the frame.
Won over token ring by being cheaper and good enough.
events.impact: The local network became commodity, which is what made the rack, the cluster, and eventually the data centre economically possible.

resources.label: Ethernet: Distributed Packet Switching for Local Computer Networks

events.title: Linux
events.summary: Announced as a hobby project that would not be big and professional, and now runs essentially every server, phone, and cloud instance.

media.alt: Open source braces motif for Linux

keyPoints: A UNIX-like kernel on commodity x86, licensed so that anyone could ship it.
The GPL made contribution the rational strategy for competing vendors.
Distributed development at a scale that produced Git as a side effect.
The cost of the operating system went to zero, which changed everyone's unit economics.
events.impact: Removed the OS licence from the cost of a server. Every cloud, every container, and every CI runner is standing on it.

events.title: VMware ESX
events.summary: Makes virtualisation work on x86 — a chip never designed to be virtualised — and turns a rack of idle servers into one busy one.
keyPoints: Binary translation worked around x86 instructions that could not be trapped.
Consolidation ratios turned hardware utilisation into a budget line.
Live migration made a running workload independent of the machine underneath it.
Intel VT-x and AMD-V later put the support in silicon.
events.impact: Decoupled the workload from the box. That decoupling is the precondition for renting compute by the hour, which is the entire cloud business model.

resources.label: Memory Resource Management in VMware ESX Server

events.title: S3 and EC2
events.summary: Storage in March, servers in August, both behind an API and a credit card — infrastructure stops being a purchase and becomes a call.
keyPoints: Capacity becomes elastic: provision in minutes, release when done.
Capital expenditure turns into operating expenditure, which changes who can start a company.
Durability and availability promises are stated as numbers in a contract.
Everything above it — autoscaling, managed services, serverless — assumes this API exists.
events.impact: Reset the default. A team's first infrastructure decision stopped being "which servers do we buy" and became "which service do we call", and the industry's cost structure followed.

events.title: Heroku
events.summary: git push to deploy — the platform-as-a-service argument, made early and made well.

events.title: Chaos engineering
events.summary: Break production on purpose, on a schedule, so that failure stops being a surprise.

events.title: Terraform
events.summary: Infrastructure declared in files and reconciled against reality — Codd's move, applied to servers.

events.title: The SRE book
events.summary: Error budgets give reliability a number, so it can be traded against velocity in the open.

events.title: Managed Kubernetes everywhere
events.summary: The control plane becomes somebody else's problem, and the orchestrator becomes the substrate.

events.title: Docker
events.summary: Wraps kernel features that had existed for years in a format people would actually use, and settles the "works on my machine" argument.
keyPoints: Namespaces and cgroups were already in Linux; the image format and the registry were the invention.
Layered, content-addressed images make builds cacheable and shippable.
The unit of deployment becomes the filesystem plus the process, not the machine.
Dependency hell moves from the server into the Dockerfile, where it is at least versioned.
events.impact: Made the build artefact identical from a laptop to production. That single guarantee is what made continuous delivery and microservices operationally realistic.

events.title: Kubernetes
events.byline: Google, from a decade of Borg
events.summary: You declare what should be running; a control loop spends the rest of its life making reality match.
keyPoints: Declarative desired state plus continuous reconciliation, rather than imperative deploys.
Scheduling, health checking, and rollout become platform concerns instead of scripts.
The extension model — custom resources and controllers — is why it ate the ecosystem.
Its complexity is real, and is mostly the complexity it absorbed from everyone's scripts.
events.impact: Became the portable substrate every cloud now offers. The reconciliation loop it popularised is the default pattern for managing anything, including infrastructure with no containers in it.

resources.label: Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg

events.title: AWS Lambda
events.summary: Bills by the millisecond of execution, which finally makes the server disappear from the part of the system that matters most: the invoice.
keyPoints: No idle cost — the unit of billing is an invocation, not an hour of capacity.
The runtime is ephemeral, which forces state out of the compute and into a service.
Cold starts are the tax, and most of the tuning advice is about them.
Event-driven composition becomes the default architecture for glue work.
events.impact: Completed the fifty-year retreat from the machine: from owning the room, to owning the box, to renting the box, to renting a fraction of a second of one.
